claims.text: Under deformation, Co-free FeNiCrMn develops an ultra-nanocrystalline or partially amorphous near-surface layer.
The near-surface layer governs the strength–ductility balance through inverse Hall–Petch effects.
The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a solid solution.
The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy generally has a coarse-grained microstructure.
Using ultra-high vacuum or an inert environment eliminates oxidation effects during loading.
Grain-boundary kinetics are active across the proposed cryogenic-to-room-temperature testing range.
The proposed temperature and strain-rate regime permits dynamic grain refinement and amorphization.
High-angle grain boundaries participate in strain-induced dynamic amorphization and grain refinement that form the near-surface layer.
Specific combinations of temperature and strain rate induce dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries.
Inverse Hall–Petch behavior of the refined or partially amorphous layer enhances ductility.
Inverse Hall–Petch behavior of the layer preserves or slightly increases strength.
Under optimal temperature and strain-rate conditions, Co-free FeNiCrMn has greater ductility than CoCrFeMnNi tested under the same conditions.
Under optimal conditions, Co-free FeNiCrMn maintains or modestly increases yield strength relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
The predicted mechanical-property transition corresponds to formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The hypothesis applies only in inert or ultra-high-vacuum environments and in a temperature–strain-rate regime permitting grain-boundary activity.
At strain rates too low to trigger dynamic processes, alternative deformation mechanisms may dominate.
The activation thresholds for dynamic amorphization in temperature and strain rate are not yet known.
Removing Co may alter the kinetics of grain refinement.
A controlled comparison should test Co-free FeNiCrMn and CoCrFeMnNi under identical inert environments and deformation protocols while measuring stress–strain response and microstructural evolution.
Failure to observe a distinct ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous layer, or failure to observe the associated mechanical-performance difference, would disfavor the proposed mechanism.
